questions.stem: Operations management is best defined as:
options: the management of the financial records and cash flow of a business
the management of the transformation of inputs into outputs
the management of the relationship between employer and employees
the process of promoting and pricing products for target customers
questions.explanation: Operations management oversees the process of turning inputs such as materials and labour into finished goods and services. Managing the employment relationship is human resource management.

questions.stem: Operations management contributes to business objectives mainly by:
options: producing quality outputs while using resources efficiently
setting the minimum wages that the business's employees must be paid
deciding which legal structure the business will operate under
resolving disputes between employees and managers in the workplace
questions.explanation: An efficient, effective operations system lowers costs and produces quality goods and services, supporting objectives such as profit and market share. Minimum wages are set by awards, not by operations management.

questions.stem: In a bakery's operations system, which is an input?
options: loaves of bread sold to customers
slicing and wrapping each finished loaf
flour, sugar and the bakers' labour
baking the dough in commercial ovens
questions.explanation: Inputs are the resources used in production, such as raw materials, labour and equipment. Baking, slicing and wrapping are processes that transform the inputs, and the loaves sold are outputs.

questions.stem: In a car-repair workshop in Mildura, which is part of the processes stage of the operations system?
options: the mechanic's tools and diagnostic equipment
the spare parts bought from a parts supplier
the repaired car returned to its satisfied owner
the mechanic diagnosing and fixing the fault
questions.explanation: Processes are the activities that transform inputs into outputs, such as diagnosing and repairing. Tools and spare parts are inputs, and the repaired car is the output.

questions.stem: A hospital is a service business. Which is an output of its operations system?
options: doctors, nurses and their medical knowledge
medical equipment, beds and prescription drugs
the surgeon performing an operation in theatre
patients who have received treatment and care
questions.explanation: Outputs are the end result of the transformation, which for a hospital is the treatment and care provided to patients. Staff and equipment are inputs, and performing the operation is a process.

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of operations in a service business, compared with a manufacturing business?
options: the service is usually produced and consumed at the same time
the output can be stored in inventory until a customer buys it
the output is tangible and can be inspected before it is purchased
there is usually little or no contact between staff and customers
questions.explanation: Services are intangible and are usually produced as they are consumed, such as a haircut, so they cannot be stored. Storable, tangible outputs that can be inspected are features of manufacturing.

questions.stem: Why is quality usually harder to control consistently in a service business than in a manufacturing business?
options: service businesses use no inputs that could be checked for quality
services are produced mainly on automated production lines
service businesses are not permitted to use quality assurance
the output is intangible and varies with each staff member and customer
questions.explanation: Because a service is intangible and delivered by people, its quality depends on who delivers it and the customer's experience, so it is hard to standardise and inspect. Service businesses still use inputs, such as staff skills and supplies, and can use quality assurance.

questions.stem: A Ballarat furniture factory and a Ballarat accounting firm both want to improve their operations. Which statement is correct?
options: the factory can hold finished stock as inventory, but the firm cannot store its services
the firm can hold finished services as inventory, but the factory cannot store furniture
neither business can measure the quality of its output in any way
both businesses produce tangible outputs that can be stored until sold
questions.explanation: Manufactured goods are tangible and can be stored, while accounting services are intangible and produced when delivered. Both businesses can still measure quality, such as defects for furniture and errors or complaints for the accounting firm.

questions.stem: Robotics in operations management involves:
options: computer forecasts of future demand for the business's products
online booking and ordering systems that customers use at any time
programmable machines doing repetitive, precise or dangerous tasks
software used to design and model new products on a computer screen
questions.explanation: Robots are programmable machines that can carry out repetitive, precise or hazardous tasks without tiring. Designing products on screen is computer-aided design.

questions.stem: Computer-aided design (CAD) is:
options: a schedule setting out the quantity of each product to be made each week
software used to design, model and modify products on a computer
a computer system that controls the machines that manufacture products
a line of robots that assembles products with little human involvement
questions.explanation: CAD lets designers create and change drawings and 3D models quickly on screen. Computer control of manufacturing machinery is computer-aided manufacturing, which students often confuse with CAD.

questions.stem: A Geelong cabinet maker sends its designs directly to a computer-controlled router that cuts each panel to size. This is an example of:
options: computer-aided design
materials requirement planning
quality assurance
computer-aided manufacturing
questions.explanation: Computer-aided manufacturing uses computers to control production machinery, here the router that cuts panels. Computer-aided design would be the software used to create the designs in the first place.

questions.stem: An online homewares retailer uses software that learns from past orders to predict demand and answers customer questions through a chatbot. This technology is:
options: a master production schedule
artificial intelligence
computer-aided design
an automated production line
questions.explanation: Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as learning from data and holding conversations. An automated production line makes physical goods with little human input.

questions.stem: A Hobart dental clinic lets patients book, change and pay for appointments on its website at any hour. Which technology strategy is it using?
options: an automated production line
online services
robotics
computer-aided manufacturing
questions.explanation: Online services let customers access a business through the internet, improving convenience and freeing staff from phone bookings. Robotics and automated lines are used to make physical products.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage for a business introducing automated production lines?
options: a slower rate of output than with manual production
high set-up costs and possible staff resistance
less consistent output quality than manual production
higher labour costs per unit of output in the long term
questions.explanation: Automation needs large up-front investment and can cause staff anxiety or redundancies, which may create resistance. Once running, automated lines usually give faster, more consistent output at lower labour cost per unit.

questions.stem: In operations management, forecasting means:
options: calculating the quantity of each material needed for each product
inspecting finished goods to find and remove any defective items
predicting future demand, often using past sales data and trends
ordering inputs only when a customer order has been received
questions.explanation: Forecasting estimates future demand so the business can plan production and materials. Calculating the materials needed for each product is materials requirement planning, which relies on the forecast and the production schedule.

questions.stem: A master production schedule shows:
options: which component materials need to be ordered from suppliers, and when
the number of defective items found in each batch that is inspected
the business's forecast of total sales across the whole industry
which finished products will be made, in what quantities and when
questions.explanation: The master production schedule is a plan of the finished products to be produced, in what quantities and over what period. Working out which components to order and when is the role of materials requirement planning.

questions.stem: A business uses a computer system that takes the master production schedule and current inventory levels to work out which components to order and when. This is:
options: Just in Time
forecasting
Total Quality Management
materials requirement planning
questions.explanation: Materials requirement planning calculates the materials needed, in the right quantities and at the right time, from the master production schedule and stock on hand. Just in Time is an approach of receiving inputs only as they are needed, not a calculation system.

questions.stem: Which sequence best shows how three materials strategies link together?
options: the master production schedule, then forecasting, then materials requirement planning
materials requirement planning, then the master production schedule, then forecasting
forecasting, then the master production schedule, then materials requirement planning
materials requirement planning, then forecasting, then the master production schedule
questions.explanation: A demand forecast is used to set the master production schedule of finished goods, and materials requirement planning then works out the inputs needed for that schedule. MRP cannot come first because it depends on the schedule.

questions.stem: Which is a key advantage of Just in Time for a business?
options: protection from supply delays by keeping large reserve stocks of inputs
much less reliance on suppliers to deliver inputs reliably and on time
less need for accurate scheduling of production and deliveries
lower inventory holding costs, such as storage and spoilage
questions.explanation: Just in Time keeps stock to a minimum by having inputs arrive as they are needed, which cuts storage costs and the risk of spoilage or obsolescence. It makes the business more reliant on suppliers and on accurate scheduling, not less.

questions.stem: A Dandenong car-parts maker uses Just in Time. A flood closes its main supplier for a week. The most likely result is that:
options: production continues normally, drawing on large buffer stocks of inputs
inventory holding costs rise sharply because of excess stock of inputs
the quality of output improves because fewer inputs are being used
production stops, because there is little or no stock of inputs on hand
questions.explanation: Under Just in Time a business holds very little inventory, so a supply disruption quickly halts production. This dependence on reliable suppliers is the main risk of the strategy.

questions.stem: Quality control involves:
options: inspecting products during or after production to find defects
a whole-of-business commitment by all staff to continuous improvement
meeting a set of quality standards certified by an independent body
building quality into every process so that defects never occur at all
questions.explanation: Quality control checks products against standards, usually at set points or at the end of production, and removes faulty items. A whole-of-business commitment to continuous improvement describes Total Quality Management.

questions.stem: A Brisbane food manufacturer has its systems audited by an independent body and is certified as meeting an international quality standard. This is an example of:
options: Total Quality Management
materials requirement planning
quality assurance
quality control
questions.explanation: Quality assurance is about meeting set quality standards, often certified by an independent body, so customers can be confident in the product. Quality control is inspection of the products themselves rather than certification of the system.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes Total Quality Management from other approaches to quality?
options: quality is the sole responsibility of the business's quality manager
every employee is responsible for quality and continuous improvement
quality is checked by specialist inspectors only at the end of the line
quality is certified once by an external auditor and then not reviewed
questions.explanation: Total Quality Management is a whole-of-organisation approach in which all employees take responsibility for quality, with a focus on customers and continuous improvement. End-of-line inspection is quality control.

questions.stem: A business moves from relying on end-of-line inspection to Total Quality Management. The key shift in its approach to quality is from:
options: internal checks by staff to certification by an external body
continuous improvement to a single inspection of finished goods
detecting defects after they occur to preventing them in every process
preventing defects in every process to detecting them after they occur
questions.explanation: End-of-line inspection finds defects once resources have been used, while Total Quality Management aims to prevent defects by improving every process. Certification by an external body is quality assurance, a different strategy.

questions.stem: Which is a weakness of relying on quality control alone?
options: defects are found after resources are used, so waste still occurs
it is unable to identify any faulty products before they leave the factory
it requires every employee in the business to join a quality circle
it requires certification by an independent body before it can be used
questions.explanation: Quality control detects faulty products, but by then materials and labour have already gone into them, so the cost of waste remains. It does identify faults, and it does not need external certification or quality circles.

questions.stem: A brewery in Castlemaine collects, cleans and refills its glass bottles. This waste minimisation strategy is:
options: recycle
Just in Time
reuse
reduce
questions.explanation: Reuse means using an item again for the same or another purpose without reprocessing it, as with refilling bottles. Recycling would involve crushing and melting the glass to make new bottles.

questions.stem: A printing firm redesigns its layouts so that each sheet of paper produces more labels and fewer offcuts. This waste minimisation strategy is:
options: recycle
quality control
reduce
reuse
questions.explanation: Reducing means cutting the amount of input used and waste created in the first place, which the new layouts do. Recycling would involve processing the offcuts into new paper.

questions.stem: A Bendigo furniture maker sends its timber offcuts to be processed into particleboard. This waste minimisation strategy is:
options: reuse
reduce
one-piece flow
recycle
questions.explanation: Recycling means processing waste materials into new materials or products, as when offcuts are turned into particleboard. Reuse would mean using the offcuts again as they are, without processing.

questions.stem: Waste minimisation can improve both the efficiency and effectiveness of operations because it:
options: cuts input costs per unit and helps meet social responsibility goals
increases the volume of inputs needed to make each unit of output
always allows the business to raise the price of its products
removes any need for the business to use quality control
questions.explanation: Using fewer inputs and creating less waste lowers costs, improving efficiency, and helps the business meet goals such as environmental responsibility, improving effectiveness. It reduces rather than increases the inputs needed.

questions.stem: In lean management, the pull strategy means that:
options: large stocks of raw materials are kept in case demand rises
goods are made in large batches before any orders arrive
production is triggered by actual customer demand
goods are produced in advance based on sales forecasts and pushed out to stores
questions.explanation: In a pull system, nothing is made until a customer order pulls it through the process, which keeps inventory low. Producing to a forecast and pushing goods out is the opposite, a push system.

questions.stem: In lean management, one-piece flow means that:
options: the whole order is completed at one station before moving to the next
a single supplier provides every input the business needs
each worker makes one complete product from start to finish
products move through each step one unit at a time, not in batches
questions.explanation: One-piece flow moves each unit straight to the next step as soon as it is finished, cutting waiting time and work-in-progress inventory. Moving whole orders at once is batch production.

questions.stem: Takt time is:
options: the time taken to deliver an order from the factory to a customer
the rate at which products must be made to meet customer demand
the total time that a finished product spends sitting in storage
the time taken to repair a machine after it has broken down
questions.explanation: Takt time sets the pace of production so that output matches customer demand, calculated as the available production time divided by customer demand. It is not a measure of storage, repair or delivery time.

questions.stem: A Sunshine Coast surfboard factory runs one 8-hour shift a day, including 30 minutes of breaks. Customer demand is 30 boards a day. What is the takt time?
options: 15 minutes per board
16 minutes per board
14 minutes per board
12 minutes per board
questions.explanation: Available time is 480 − 30 = 450 minutes, and 450 ÷ 30 = 15 minutes per board. Forgetting to subtract the breaks gives 480 ÷ 30 = 16 minutes.

questions.stem: The lean principle of zero defects aims to:
options: reduce the business's stock of inputs to zero at the end of each day
build quality in so that faults are prevented at their source
accept a small, fixed level of defects as a normal part of production
check every finished product at the end of the line for faults
questions.explanation: Zero defects aims to get products right the first time by fixing problems where they start, so no faulty products are made or passed on. Checking finished products at the end of the line is quality control.

questions.stem: A Wodonga bike-parts factory used to make parts in large batches and store them. It now makes each part only when an order arrives and passes each unit straight to the next step. Which lean strategies has it adopted?
options: takt and one-piece flow
pull and one-piece flow
takt and zero defects
pull and zero defects
questions.explanation: Making parts only when an order arrives is pull, and passing each unit straight to the next step is one-piece flow. Nothing in the case describes setting a production pace to match demand, which is takt, or building in quality, which is zero defects.

questions.stem: Which is a corporate social responsibility consideration relating to the inputs of an operations system?
options: using materials requirement planning to schedule component orders
setting a takt time so that production matches customer demand
sourcing timber only from certified sustainable forests
inspecting finished products for defects before they are dispatched
questions.explanation: Choosing environmentally sustainable inputs, such as certified timber, is a CSR consideration for inputs. Inspection, MRP and takt time are strategies to improve operations but are not mainly about social responsibility.

questions.stem: A Gippsland dairy invests in equipment to capture methane from its effluent ponds and use it to generate electricity. This reflects corporate social responsibility mainly in relation to:
options: its materials requirement planning
the waste generated from its processes
its global outsourcing of production
its master production schedule
questions.explanation: Capturing methane cuts the emissions produced by the dairy's processes, reducing the waste it generates. Outsourcing and scheduling are not involved in this decision.

questions.stem: Global sourcing of inputs means:
options: selling the business's finished products to customers in other countries
buying inputs from suppliers in other countries
building and running the business's own factory in another country
contracting an overseas business to perform one of the business's functions
questions.explanation: Global sourcing is purchasing raw materials, components or other inputs from overseas suppliers, often for lower cost or better quality. Running your own factory abroad is overseas manufacture.

questions.stem: An Australian clothing brand builds, owns and runs its own factory in Vietnam. This is:
options: overseas manufacture
global outsourcing
global sourcing of inputs
Just in Time
questions.explanation: Overseas manufacture means the business itself produces its goods in another country, keeping ownership and control of the operation. Global outsourcing would involve contracting another business to make the clothing.

questions.stem: A Melbourne bank contracts a company in the Philippines to run its customer call centre. Which statement is correct?
options: this is global outsourcing, because another business performs the function
this is overseas manufacture, because the bank owns and runs the call centre
this is global sourcing of inputs, because raw materials are bought overseas
this is a pull strategy, because calls are answered only when customers ring
questions.explanation: Global outsourcing is contracting an overseas business to carry out a function that the business would otherwise do itself, such as a call centre. The bank does not own the call centre, so it is not overseas manufacture.

questions.stem: Which is a risk for a business that uses global outsourcing?
options: less control over quality and working conditions at the provider
higher labour costs than the business would pay in Australia
the need to build and staff its own new factory in another country
reduced access to specialist skills that are not available locally
questions.explanation: Because another business performs the work overseas, the outsourcing business has less direct control over quality, ethics and working conditions. Building its own factory overseas is part of overseas manufacture, not outsourcing.
